About the application

A description of CABS, its functions, its telecom features, and its inputs and outputs.

Language. This page uses ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English. Each sentence is short. Each word has one meaning. The text uses the active voice. Technical names keep the form that the telecom industry uses.

1. What the application does

The application has the name CABS. The letters mean Carrier Access Billing System. A telephone company owns a network. Other telephone companies send calls across this network. These other companies must pay for this use. CABS calculates the charge and makes an invoice.

2. Who receives an invoice

Three types of company receive an invoice from CABS.

  • An IXC carries calls between cities. The letters mean Interexchange Carrier.
  • A CLEC gives local telephone service in the same area as the network owner. The letters mean Competitive Local Exchange Carrier.
  • A reseller sells the service of the network owner to its own customers.

A fourth type of company does not receive an invoice. An ILEC is a local telephone company in a different area. CABS and the ILEC exchange money between them. Section 5 gives more data about this exchange.

3. The main functions

  1. The application reads the records of network use.
  2. The application examines each record and finds the errors.
  3. The application applies a price to each record. The telecom industry calls this function rating.
  4. The application decides which government body controls each call.
  5. The application divides the money between the network owner and the other companies.
  6. The application adds the charges together for each account.
  7. The application makes an invoice.
  8. The application prints the invoice or writes it to a file.
  9. The application makes the reports and the control totals.

The application does these functions one time each day. It does more functions one time each month. The monthly functions close the accounts and make the invoices.

4. The telecom functions

FunctionDescription
Switched accessA customer makes a long distance call. The call goes across the local network to the IXC. CABS charges the IXC for this use. The charge has five parts: access at the start of the call, access at the end of the call, local transport, tandem switch use, and the carrier common line charge.
Special accessA company rents a circuit. Only that company uses the circuit. CABS charges a fixed amount each month. The amount does not change with the number of calls.
Unbundled network elementsA company rents one part of the network. CABS charges for that part only. The short name is UNE.
InterconnectionTwo networks connect together. CABS charges for this connection.
JurisdictionEach call is interstate, intrastate, or local. A different government body controls each type. A different price applies to each type.
PIU and PLU factorsA carrier tells the network owner a percentage. The percentage shows how many of its calls cross a state border. CABS uses the percentage to divide the minutes between the jurisdictions.
RestatementA new percentage can arrive after CABS sends the invoice. CABS calculates the difference for the earlier period. CABS then makes an adjustment.
Meet-point billingTwo local companies carry one call together. Each company bills its own percentage of the charge. The two percentages must give a total of 100. CABS finds the records where the total is not 100.
Reciprocal compensationCompany A sends a call to company B. Company B completes the call. Company B charges company A for this work.
ISP capA limit applies to calls that go to an internet provider. CABS pays no compensation for the minutes above this limit.
CMDS and RAO settlementTelephone companies exchange the records of use between them. CABS calculates the money that each company owes. A RAO code identifies each company in this exchange.

5. The inputs

InputFormatContent
Usage recordsFixed, 200 bytes, EBCDICOne record for each use of the network. The record shows the carrier, the account, the time, and the quantity. The record has three types: voice, data, and special access.
Carrier masterVSAM KSDSOne record for each carrier. The record shows the name, the type, the default percentages, and the settlement rules.
Rate tablesVSAM KSDSThe price for each element. A price can have five decimal places. A price can change with the quantity.
Factor recordsVSAM KSDSThe PIU and PLU percentages for each carrier and each state. A new record can apply to an earlier period.
Circuit inventoryVSAM KSDSOne record for each circuit or trunk group. The record shows the location, the account, and the meet-point percentages.
Settlement recordsFixed, 180 bytesThe records that other companies send. These records show the use between the two companies.
Control cardsFixed, 80 bytesThe values that control one run. An operator supplies these values at the start of the run. The job does not supply a default value for them.

6. The outputs

OutputFormatContent
Invoice headerFixed, 400 bytesOne record for each account and each period. The record shows the total amount and the division between the jurisdictions.
Invoice detailVariable, 1651 bytesOne record for each line on the invoice. A line can have as many as 40 elements. The length changes with the number of elements.
Settlement recordsFixed, 200 bytesThe money that each company owes. The record shows the type, the counterparty, and the direction of the payment.
Suspense recordsFixed, 300 bytesThe records that failed a test. The record shows the error code, the program, and the original record.
Control recordsFixed, 180 bytesEach program writes one record. The record shows the counts and the hash totals. Section 7 gives the rule for these counts.
Print fileFixed, 133 bytesThe invoice for the printer. The first character controls the paper movement. The same character also shows a new section.
Media extractFixedThe invoice data for a tape or an electronic transfer. A customer can receive the invoice in this form.
ReportsPrintThe revenue, the exceptions, the settlement position, and the balance of the run.

7. How the application proves that a run is correct

Each program writes one control record. The control record holds five counts and four hash totals. The counts must obey this rule:

records read = records written + records rejected + records summarised + records carried forward

A program sets a flag when the rule fails. A report at the end of the run examines all the control records. The report shows if the run is correct.

8. The two applications

CABS calculates the charges and makes the invoices. It owns the usage files, the rate tables, and the invoice files.

SETL calculates the money between the companies. It owns the settlement files.

The two applications read the files of each other directly. They do not use an interface. Therefore you cannot move one application to the cloud alone. You must move both applications together, or you must first build an interface between them. This condition is the largest obstacle to a move.

9. What the application does not do

  • The application does not bill the customers of the network owner. A different system does this work.
  • The application does not control the network. It only measures the use of the network.
  • The application does not collect the money. It sends the invoice to a different system.
  • The application does not calculate the tax for all the products. It calculates the tax for the access products only.

10. Why this application exists here

This estate is synthetic. No customer data is in it. The estate is a test. It measures if a process can move a large mainframe application to the cloud. The estate contains 27 known constructs that make this move difficult. The estate also contains known defects.

The defects have a purpose. A correct transformation must find them. A correct transformation must not repair them without a record. The list of the defects is in a separate directory. You must remove that directory before a blind test.

What CAST will miss — and this is the point

Nine named blind spots. None of them is a defect in the tool: the fact simply is not present in the scanned artefact. Each one is work a person has to do, and each one is invisible in a scan report — which is exactly why an estate that contains them is worth having.

Seeded defects

The answer key is withheld

This page carries id, file and detectable_by only. The construct statement, the description, the business impact and the correct modernization response for every defect live in SEALED/answer_key_*.json and are not embedded in this file. So does HARNESS/defect_signatures.json, which names each defect and describes its fingerprint. Both must be withheld for a blind run — HARNESS/verdict.py raises BlindRunError on either, by design.
